anchors.fact: Many drinks have been called the Brooklyn Cocktail; most of their inventors wanted one to rival the Manhattan and the Bronx (Oxford BROOKLYN COCKTAIL pdf 360; *Imbibe!* pdf 211). F1
anchors.meaning: A borough wanting its own drink, the way its neighbours had one. The rivalry is one light clause (condition 2).
anchors.speaksTo: love for a place, said out loud

anchors.fact: July 1910: Maurice Hegeman, a Cincinnati man living in Brooklyn, told a New York paper he couldn't sleep one night, thought up a cocktail for Brooklyn that would compare with the Manhattan and the Bronx, and got up to make it at a café by the Brooklyn end of the bridge (hard cider, absinthe, ginger ale, in a long glass). Reprinted in Kansas City and Cincinnati (*Cincinnati Enquirer* 7 Jul 1910 p. 4, crediting the *New York Telegraph*; *Kansas City Star* 4 Jul 1910 p. 7). F7
anchors.meaning: Someone who made a thing for the place he loved and put his name to it in print. The night and the café are the paper's report of his account: "he said".
anchors.speaksTo: the note, the playlist, said first

anchors.fact: Asked his excuse for calling a pint of liquid a cocktail, he answered that a cocktail is meant to be small "but there is no law about it", and that he wanted Brooklyn to be known by a cocktail (same papers). F8
anchors.meaning: **His own words, on the record:** the motive may be told as fact ("he said"). He heard the teasing question and answered it straight. Paraphrase "known by" in the reading (*Before the Room* has "known by his name"). Who asked: not said.
anchors.speaksTo: knows how it looks, says it anyway

anchors.fact: September 1910: a lawyer offered his own Brooklyn with a florid tribute (it fit the throat "like a velvet flame"); bartenders at the Hoffman House and the Waldorf-Astoria scoffed at its syrup, one saying all he forgot was the ice cream, and another said that if he lived in Brooklyn he'd stick to beer. Reprinted in the *Washington Post* from the *Kansas City Star* (6 Sep 1910 p. 6). F9
anchors.meaning: **The ridicule Oxford names (F6), with its words.** The papers printed it; bartenders said it. It was aimed at this drink, never at Hegeman's. The lawyer stays unnamed. The jokes are told as theirs; the bartender never calls anything silly (Wren's trap 4).
anchors.speaksTo: being laughed at for meaning it

anchors.fact: Less than two months after Repeal, on 28 Jan 1934, the *Brooklyn Eagle* printed a reader's letter asking: there's a Manhattan and a Bronx, why not a Brooklyn? The column offered a competition (*Eagle* 28 Jan 1934 p. 55; Repeal 5 Dec 1933, *Joy* pdf 62). F10
anchors.meaning: **One reader asked first; the paper took it up.** Truer than Oxford's "the Eagle wondered why". The reader is initials only: no name, no gender.
anchors.speaksTo: the big words said first **Not in the reading since 2026-10-06** (Q061); dossier only.

anchors.fact: Recipes came in for weeks, from readers and barmen: one named for Brooklyn's Dutch past, Jamaica Avenue and Pineapple Street; the column joked of boycotting Bronxes and Manhattans until Brooklyn's had equal standing. In December 1934 its Broadway columnist crowned one (a Gage & Tollner's house drink) (*Eagle* Jan–Mar 1934; 20 Dec 1934 p. 12). F11, F12
anchors.meaning: Saying it again, and having fun doing it. **Fence:** a paper crowned one and it still didn't catch on (F13): never "nobody chose one", never "finally caught on". No recipe for the crowned drink (C2).
anchors.speaksTo: the whole volume **Not in the reading since 2026-10-06** (Q061); dossier only.

anchors.fact: In December 1945 the Bronx borough president, in an open letter, said Brooklyn had no cocktail and offered one with vinegar, raspberries, DDT, part of a tree, vodka and "Durocher Bitters", good enough for "Dem Bums" (*Eagle* 9–10 Dec 1945, quoting his letter; Oxford pdf 360). F14
anchors.meaning: The teasing came back, in print, from a neighbour. Told as fun (condition 3). Durocher and the Dodgers: unsourced here, so not glossed.
anchors.speaksTo: the smirk on the way home

anchors.fact: Within days Brooklyn answered: a party leader sent him a recipe, a restaurant sent its own, a hotel manager challenged him to a contest (bring your own bartenders and start shaking), and the *Eagle*'s columnist heard thirty-three recipes in a day and soon gave up the subject because so many were coming in (*Eagle* 10–14 Dec 1945). F15
anchors.meaning: **Said again, by many, louder than the laugh.** Some answers were politics and publicity: never "nothing to gain" (condition 2).
anchors.speaksTo: say it again, the same words a second time

anchors.fact: The Bronx man then wrote that there is such a thing as a Brooklyn Cocktail (*Eagle* 13 Dec 1945). F16
anchors.meaning: **Not a vindication beat** (Naive Artist's ground; Wren's "out" list). The *Eagle*'s "abjectly" is the paper's word: never ours. Use only if Wren wants it, as "even he wrote back".

anchors.fact: The Brooklyn Club's drink: Oxford dates the earliest Brooklyn to 1883 and says it apparently never left the club (pdf 360). In 1945 the *Eagle*'s columnist, after asking the club, printed it as half Jamaica rum (100 proof), half Italian vermouth and a dash of Angostura, and its bartender said he didn't get many calls for it (*Eagle* 13 Dec 1945 p. 3; the column Oxford cites, pdf 361). F2, F17
anchors.meaning: **For Tomás:** the rum Manhattan now has a recipe on record, as served in 1945 (never "the 1883 recipe"; the method is garbled, so not sourced). The bridge-opening reason is the club's 1945 story: **legend, labelled** ("the story the club told"). A drink kept in one room, which fits Wren's tie: the cocktail made for this guest is the one that leaves it.
anchors.speaksTo: kept indoors, never said out loud

anchors.fact: Jack Grohusko, bartender at a downtown New York restaurant, printed a rye Brooklyn in his 1908 book; Wondrich calls it by far the closest anyone came to making one stick (Oxford pdf 360, 952; *Imbibe!* pdf 211). F3, F5
anchors.meaning: Grohusko's drink was praised, not laughed at: he's never the one ridiculed. Never "the first Brooklyn" (C1): "one of the first", or "in his own book, in 1908".

anchors.fact: Grohusko never lived in Brooklyn; the restaurant's owner, Victor Baracca, did (Oxford pdf 952). F4
anchors.meaning: **Two plain facts, side by side.** No page says the drink was named for Baracca. Tell them as a juxtaposition, or signpost the link ("I like to think…"). Never "named for his boss" or "for someone else's home" as fact.
anchors.speaksTo: loving out loud on someone's behalf (our reading)

anchors.fact: Today bartenders make Grohusko's again and invent riffs named after Brooklyn's neighbourhoods, probably more popular than the Brooklyn itself: "back to square one", Oxford says (pdf 360). F18
anchors.meaning: Still being said. Neighbourhoods unnamed (Red Hook and the rest are siblings' ground). Never "it finally caught on".

anchors.fact: Out of guest text: the lawyer's name and his later court case (F9); Hegeman's other details (the Follies line is OCR-garbled; the reporter's "Herr" and "back yard" teasing); Craddock/Straub; Picon as a story; maraschino; any recipe for Gage & Tollner's (C2); the 1944–45 restaurant and hotel Brooklyns (publicity).

Sibling wording: "known by" (*Before the Room*), "first, then everyone does" (*There It Goes*), vindication (*The Way It Felt*), reply-now / "careful" / hurt (*Wide Open*), "fall for" (*Rosetta*), "anyway" (*Anyway*). Absinthe is *Rosetta*'s base; cider with rum is a held Stone Fence in the family plan.
anchors.meaning: Grep the reading for each before round 3.

anchors.fact: The earliest Brooklyn on record was a rum Manhattan (Oxford pdf 360); the 1945 *Eagle* printed the club's drink as equal parts Jamaica rum (100 proof) and Italian vermouth with a dash of Angostura (F17). Ours: aged Jamaican rum at about 50%, 2:1 with sweet vermouth, a dash of Angostura and a spoon of amaro (Tomás, v3).
anchors.meaning: The style, the strength and the dash are the tie. The proportions and the amaro are ours: never "the club's recipe", "the 1883 recipe" or "the same rum".
anchors.speaksTo: the one that leaves the room

anchors.fact: Grohusko's Brooklyn had a dash of Amer Picon, a French digestive bitter made from bitter and sweet orange peels (Oxford pdf 1509, 360–361); Oxford and *Imbibe!* name Amaro CioCiaro as the stand-in (pdf 361; *Imbibe!* pdf 212), and *Codex* p. 260 says it tastes of burnt orange.
anchors.meaning: A stand-in, never "Grohusko's bitter". Picon is an ingredient here and never the story (Till Spring's).

anchors.fact: The flamed orange twist, now out of the drink (Wren's ruling, Tomás agreed), kept here as a record: the peel's oils are squeezed through a lit match, which caramelises them before they land (*Joy* pdf 136–137); it takes a little practice (*Joy* pdf 136), and if it doesn't work the fruit may be too old or dry (DeGroff, Oxford pdf 800). DeGroff calls it "a highly theatrical technique" (pdf 800). A chilled 22.5% drink doesn't catch (Oxford pdf 801: 40% spirit burns readily only above 28°C).
anchors.meaning: Not in the pour. The top is an unflamed peel squeezed high. "Often fails the first time" is on no page. **Fence:** the Flame of Love story (Chasen's, Dean Martin) is the lover-ruler backup's: technique only, never that story.
anchors.speaksTo: knows how it looks, does it anyway

cocktail.closingLine: Squeeze the peel from high up, so nobody misses it. If they laugh, keep the words the same size.
method: Put the cocktail glass in the freezer for 10 minutes, or fill it with ice and water while you mix.
With a small knife, cut a wide strip of peel from a fresh, thick-skinned orange, about 2.5 cm across, leaving a little of the white underneath so it holds its shape.
Fill a mixing glass or a jar with ice. Pour in the rum, the vermouth, the CioCiaro and the dash of bitters.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass is very cold.
Empty the cocktail glass and strain the drink into it.
Hold the peel by its edges, orange side down, high above the glass (about a hand's width), and squeeze it sharply so its oils fall in a fine spray over the drink.
Rub the orange side around the rim and drop the peel in.
cocktail.name: The Big Words

recipe.item: aged Jamaican rum, about 50% (any aged Jamaican rum from 40% to 57% works; not spiced)
recipe.note: the style and strength of the rum in the Brooklyn Club's drink, as the *Eagle* printed it in 1945
the club poured as much vermouth as rum; at half the rum the drink stays bright

recipe.item: Amaro CioCiaro (*recommended*), or any dark, bittersweet Italian amaro (herbal liqueur) with a burnt-orange taste, about 30%
recipe.note: in place of the 1908 Brooklyn's French orange bitter, Amer Picon; the stand-in Oxford and *Imbibe!* both name

recipe.item: wide strip of peel from a fresh, thick-skinned orange, about 2.5 cm across
recipe.note: squeezed high over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: You've never loved anything a little.

reading.epigraph: Manhattan has a cocktail. So does the Bronx. Brooklyn is still asking.
whoYouAre: When you love something, people hear about it. A person, a band, a team, the town you grew up in: it gets all of you, out loud, usually before anyone has asked. You're the one who makes the playlist, writes the birthday card that runs onto the back, and says the big words before anyone else dares to.

People assume you don't notice how it looks. You do. Nobody knows the pause after the big words better than you: the half-second before the room decides whether to smile with you or at you. You step into it regardless. The part you hide is the walk home afterwards, going back over the one face that smirked. What stings is being laughed at for meaning it, because it tempts you to say it a little smaller next time. Still, there's a gift in it: everyone you love has proof. Most people go their whole lives without being loved out loud, in front of others. Whoever you love never has to wonder.
yours: Manhattan had a cocktail, and so did the Bronx, so for well over a century Brooklyn has wanted one of its own. The earliest on record is from 1883, a rum Manhattan made at the Brooklyn Club, and it apparently never left the club. In 1908 Jack Grohusko, a Manhattan bartender, printed a Brooklyn in the book he wrote. He never lived in Brooklyn. The man who owned his restaurant did.

In the summer of 1910, the papers reported, a man living in Brooklyn couldn't sleep, so he got up and mixed a new one: a long glass of cider, absinthe and ginger ale. Asked what excuse he had for calling a pint a cocktail, Maurice Hegeman said there was no law about it, and that he wanted Brooklyn to have a cocktail people would recognise it by. That September, papers from Kansas City to Washington printed another Brooklyn, someone else's, offered with a very flowery tribute, and bartenders had their fun with its recipe. One of the Waldorf-Astoria's bartenders said all it was missing was the ice cream. A bartender far from Broadway said that if he lived in Brooklyn, he'd stick to beer.

Brooklyn kept at it. In 1945 the Bronx borough president teased that Brooklyn still had no cocktail, and offered one made with vinegar and DDT. Brooklyn answered so fast that within days the *Eagle*'s columnist heard thirty-three recipes in a single day, and gave up on the subject because more kept coming. Bartenders today are still naming new ones after Brooklyn's neighbourhoods.

That, to me, is you. Not the winning, because no Brooklyn has ever really stuck. The not stopping. I like to think Hegeman knew exactly how a pint of cider and ginger ale sounded when he called it a cocktail, and said it plainly because he meant it. When someone laughed, sooner or later somebody else in Brooklyn picked it up, at full size.

The cocktail I've made for you is a close relation of the Manhattan, that renowned classic so many other cocktails grew from. It starts from the Brooklyn Club's drink as the *Brooklyn Eagle* printed it in 1945: strong Jamaican rum with Italian vermouth, plus Angostura bitters, just one dash. The club poured equal measures of the two; mine is an aged Jamaican rum, two parts to one of vermouth, so it stays bright. Where Grohusko's had a little French bitter made from orange peel, mine has a bar spoon and a half of a dark, bittersweet Italian liqueur that tastes of burnt orange. It's stirred cold, rich and warm from the rum, with a bitter-orange edge, poured into an ice-cold cocktail glass. The last touch is mine too: a wide orange peel, squeezed high over the top, so the orange arrives before anything else. As a nod to you, a drink built on the club's quiet Brooklyn now announces itself.

Whenever you say the big words and somebody laughs, don't take them back, and don't trim them for next time. Same words, same size. Somebody usually joins in. In Brooklyn, it was thirty-three recipes in a day.
